extracted.intended_audience: school and college administrators, Title IX coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, and policymakers responsible for implementing Title IX grievance processes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards for designing and carrying out Title IX grievance processes in educational institutions, including requirements for remedies, evidence evaluation, training, and procedural safeguards. Applies to K-12 and higher education recipients implementing §106.45 grievance procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable treatment of parties (§106.45(b)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must treat complainants and respondents equitably during the grievance process: treating complainants equitably means providing remedies where a respondent is determined responsible; treating respondents equitably means imposing disciplinary sanctions or other actions that are not supportive measures only after following the §106.45 grievance process. The final regulations replace the phrase “due process protections” with “a grievance process that complies with §106.45.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text clarifies that equitable treatment does not mean privileging one party; the grievance process is of equal benefit to complainants and respondents. Changes: revised wording to use “equal access” and “determination of responsibility.” The provision is intended to ensure remedies for complainants and procedural protections for respondents while avoiding creating a vague general ‘equitableness’ standard across other provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies designed to restore or preserve equal access
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a grievance results in a determination of responsibility, the complainant must be given remedies designed to restore or preserve the complainant's equal access to the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regs use the phrase “equal access.” Remedies may consist of the individualized services illustratively listed as “supportive measures” in §106.30 but are not limited by the constraints of supportive measures; remedies may burden the respondent and may be punitive or disciplinary in nature. Recipients are responsible for the effective implementation of remedies (§106.45(b)(7)(iv)). The Department declines to require particular lists of remedies or to delete qualifying language like “designed to.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator responsibility for effective implementation of remedies (§106.45(b)(7)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX Coordinators must be responsible for the effective implementation of remedies designed to restore or preserve a complainant's equal access to education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies that the burden of implementing remedies rests on the recipient (not the complainant). Effective implementation is part of evaluating whether remedies were reasonably designed and carried out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removal exception with post-removal notice/challenge (§106.44)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may remove a respondent from the recipient's education program or activity without undergoing the §106.45 grievance process where an individualized risk assessment shows the respondent poses a threat to any person's physical health or safety, provided the respondent receives post-removal notice and an opportunity to challenge the removal decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency removal and supportive measures may be necessary even while preserving the grievance process; commenters had argued tensions between emergency removal and equitable treatment provisions, but the regs permit removal as an individualized safety measure with post-removal procedural rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures: wide latitude (§106.30 and §106.45(b)(1)(i) language)
rubrics_metrics.description: The §106.30 definition of “supportive measures” gives recipients wide latitude to take actions to support a complainant while refraining from imposing disciplinary sanctions against a respondent; final regs added phrase “or other actions that are not supportive measures as defined in §106.30” to §106.45(b)(1)(i) to clarify scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures can be broad but are distinct from remedies that may be punitive. The regs do not require recipients to list off-campus resources, but require describing range of supportive measures available (§106.45(b)(1)(ix)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-neutral grievance process
rubrics_metrics.description: The grievance process and Title IX implementation must be neutral with respect to sex; Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate benefits persons without regard to sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sex-neutral framework is intended to prevent bias and avoid improper generalizations (e.g., 'women as victims' or 'men as perpetrators') from affecting evaluation of particular allegations. Background knowledge about dynamics of sexual violence is permitted but cannot be applied in a way that injects bias or lack of impartiality into the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of non-responsibility until conclusion (§106.45(b)(1)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondents are afforded a presumption of non-responsibility until the conclusion of the grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption is compatible with objective evaluation of evidence and does not mean treating respondents as inherently credible; it supports impartial fact-finding and prevents prejudging facts based on party status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evaluation of all relevant evidence (§106.45(b)(1)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients' investigations and adjudications must be based on an objective evaluation of the evidence available in a particular case; relevant evidence includes both inculpatory and exculpatory evidence whether obtained from a party or another source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Does not require corroborating or 'objective' evidence beyond available relevant evidence (e.g., parties' statements suffice in some cases). The provision seeks to avoid bias, does not permit endless delay (timeframes constrain investigation), and leaves flexibility to recipients regarding admissibility rules while requiring relevance as the governing standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on credibility determinations based on party status
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators and decision-makers must not draw credibility conclusions based on a person's status as a complainant or respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regs reject allowing credibility assessments 'in part' based solely on status; determinations of credibility must be grounded in objective evaluation of evidence and not on inferences from party status. Understanding parties' interests and stakes is permitted, but stakes alone do not reflect truthfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirements on relevance, bias, and evidentiary issues (§106.45(b)(1)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX personnel (investigators, decision-makers) are required to be well trained in conducting a grievance process compliant with §106.45, including training on relevance, application of rape shield protections, and prohibition against bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regs added a specific training obligation concerning relevance; recipients may adopt additional training (e.g., rules of evidence, evaluating credibility). Training is intended to promote impartiality and competence in evidence evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence inspection, review, and investigative report (§106.45(b)(5)(vi) & (vii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must make all evidence directly related to the allegations available to the parties for inspection and review, including inculpatory and exculpatory evidence; recipients must create an investigative report that fairly summarizes all relevant evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may review and respond to the investigative report; the investigator is obligated to gather evidence whether or not the recipient intends to rely on it. Parties can challenge relevance determinations in written responses, hearings, and on appeal for procedural irregularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker must explain evidentiary basis in written determination (§106.45(b)(7)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-makers must lay out the evidentiary basis for the conclusions reached in a written determination regarding responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement supports transparency and allows for meaningful appeals based on the evidentiary reasoning underlying determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on use of privileged information (§106.45(b)(1)(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: The recipient is precluded from using evidence that would result in disclosure of information protected by a legally recognized privilege (e.g., attorney-client).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regs explicitly add this prohibition; parties must not be forced to disclose privileged communications as part of the grievance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rape shield protections: prior sexual behavior generally irrelevant (§106.45(b)(6) referenced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions and evidence about a complainant's prior sexual behavior are deemed irrelevant with two enumerated exceptions and are generally precluded from use in the grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regs include rape shield limits; training on relevance includes application of these protections. The two exceptions exist but are narrowly constrained in the regs (not fully detailed in this chunk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator discretion on relevance with party challenge and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators determine what evidence is relevant and must summarize relevant evidence in the investigative report, but parties have equal opportunity to challenge relevance determinations in written responses, at hearings, and on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The investigator need not rely on every piece of evidence but must gather evidence directly related to the allegations. Parties can argue about relevance and persuasiveness; failure to objectively evaluate relevant evidence can be a ground for appeal as procedural irregularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to complete grievance process within reasonably prompt timeframes (§106.45(b)(1)(v))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must conclude the grievance process within designated, reasonably prompt timeframes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constraint prevents indefinite delay while allowing sufficient time to gather and evaluate available evidence; it balances thorough investigation with timely resolution.
